lines.text: You're desperately thirsty, and you get to pick one of two cups. One is muddy brown. The other is crystal clear.
Most people grab the clear one right away. But in the real world, clear water can make you just as sick as muddy water.
Because the most dangerous things in water are usually the things your eyes can't see.
Today, Zero has to find drinking water. And he has to choose right.
Yesterday, Zero explored the valley, drew a map in the dirt, and picked the site for his first base.
But the whole day, he didn't drink a single drop.
Morning of day two. A dry mouth, a slight headache, dark urine. The dehydration warning signs he learned yesterday are showing up.
Today's goal: find the least risky source of water, and find a way to get it up to his mouth.
The catch: no fire yet. No pot. No container. Just two hands, and a map on the ground.
So today, Zero can't boil water. All he can do is choose the source as smartly as possible.
Zero studies his map. In this valley, there are five kinds of places with water.
The wide, slow river. The fast rapids. Muddy puddles on the clay bank. A still pool in the jungle. And the waterfall upstream.
But before he sets off, he needs something to scoop water with. Zero picks a big leaf at the jungle edge.
He folds it into a cone and pinches the tip. With nothing to cut it, the edge tears and goes ragged. But it works.
The closest stop is the river. Zero scoops some water up to take a look.
It's fairly clear, with no smell. But here's the problem: how do you know it's clean enough, with no way to measure anything?
All Zero has are his eyes, his nose, and an understanding of where dirt in water comes from.
Let's magnify a single drop of water. What's mixed into water falls into two big groups.
The first group is sediment: soil, sand, and bits of leaves. That's what makes water cloudy, and we can see it.
The second group is tiny living things, like bacteria, viruses, and some parasites. Some of them cause diarrhea, and serious illness.
The smallest thing the human eye can see is about a tenth of a millimeter. Roughly the thickness of a hair.
But most bacteria are only about a thousandth of a millimeter. Dozens of times thinner than a hair.
And viruses are much smaller still. Even with lots of germs in it, water can still look perfectly clear.
That's why clear water only tells you there's little sediment. It does not tell you the water is safe.
Even today, around the world, waterborne diseases still make huge numbers of people sick every year.
So where do these germs come from? Mostly from human and animal droppings, dead animals, and dirty water draining into rivers and ponds.
Animals that drink from a stream or cross it can leave germs behind. Then the current carries them downstream.
And in warm, still water, some germs can multiply easily, because nothing carries them away.
So Zero comes up with four simple questions to compare water sources.
One: is it flowing, or still? Two: what's upstream? Three: are there signs of animals? And four: color, smell, and anything floating in it.
These questions don't make water any safer. But they help you pick the source that's less risky.
Back at the river. The water keeps flowing. That's a pass. But then Zero looks upstream.
He sees tracks from several animals coming down to the water's edge. This stretch of river is where animals come to drink.
So the river gets a middle score. Usable if there's no other choice, but not the best source.
Second stop: a puddle by the clay bank. The water is murky brown, warm from the sun, and going nowhere.
Zero dips his leaf in. The water is full of sediment, and it smells strongly of mud.
Leave it, and the sediment will sink to the bottom. But the germs in warm, still water aren't going anywhere.
This puddle fails almost every test. Still, warm, and murky. Zero doesn't drink a drop.
Third stop: the rapids. The water is strong, and constantly churning.
But yesterday, Zero already noted that the rocks here are slippery and the current is dangerous. Scooping water here, he's more likely to fall in than to get sick.
Fourth stop: deep in the jungle, Zero finds a small pool under the trees.
The water is so clear you can see the leaves on the bottom. It's cooler than the river, and perfectly calm.
No sediment. No smell. Judging by eye alone, this pool beats every source he's seen all day.
Zero kneels down, fills his leaf cup, and lifts it up to drink.
But before the water reaches his mouth, he sees something moving in it.
Tiny things, wriggling up and down, rhythmically. These are mosquito larvae.
Zero pours the water out immediately, and looks around the edge of the pool.
The mud around the pool is covered in animal tracks. And there are droppings nearby.
No water flows in. No water flows out. Animals from all over the jungle drink here, and everything that goes in, stays in.
On top of that, leaves that fall in slowly rot on the bottom.
The larvae tell us this water has been still for days, because mosquitoes love to lay their eggs in standing water.
And the clearness? That's just sediment settling to the bottom. The invisible germs are all still floating around.
The clearest water of all turned out to fail the hardest.
Today's lesson: clear water does not mean clean water.
Zero goes back over his questions. Low-risk water has to keep flowing, and whatever is upstream has to be as clean as possible.
That means going as high as he can. Upstream.
He follows the river all the way up to the waterfall, at the head of the valley.
Even the waterfall gets its water from a stream up above, where we can't see what's there. But then Zero notices something else.
On the rock wall beside him, water is seeping out of a crack in the stone. Drip. By drip.
This is groundwater. Water that has soaked down through soil and rock for a long time.
On the way, the soil and rock filter out sediment and some of the germs. So this kind of water is often less risky than surface water.
But not always. Groundwater can be contaminated too, if dirt and waste soak down into it.
The water dripping here never ran across ground where animals walk.
Zero sets his leaf cup under the drip, careful not to let the leaf touch the moss, or the ground.
Because however good the source is, if the container is dirty, the water gets dirty too.
After a while, the cup fills up. Clear, no smell, and from a place animals can't reach.
The torn leaf cup still leaks a little. Zero has to hold it with both hands.
Time for the four questions. Always flowing. The source is solid rock. No animal signs. No color, no smell. It passes them all.
Zero is out of options, so he takes one small sip. It's the least risky choice he has today, but it is still not safe. Please don't copy this.
In real life, always boil natural water, or treat it with a proven method, before you drink it.
And when Zero has fire and a pot one day, that's the first thing he'll do.
Zero also notes one more source: rain, caught straight from the sky on a clean leaf, before it runs over the ground. That's low risk too.
Zero heads back to base, and adds what he learned to his map.
Drips from the rock: lowest risk, but it still needs boiling. The river: only when necessary. The rapids: too dangerous. And the still pool and the mud puddle: never drink.
So, today's lesson. Clearness only tells you about sediment. What tells you more about the risk is where the water came from, and what it passed through.
Unlocked: a water source map, and four questions for choosing water.
But all day, Zero had to tear leaves by hand. The edges are ragged, and water keeps leaking out.
With one sharp thing, everything would be so much easier. But where do you find something sharp, in a world with nothing but rocks?
Next time, Zero turns an ordinary rock into a sharp stone flake.
